source.title: Fast and Simplex: 2-Simplicial Attention in Triton
source.authors: Aurko Roy; Timothy Chou; Sai Surya Duvvuri; Sijia Chen; Jie-Cao Yu; Xiao-Dong Wang; M. Zaheer; Rohan Anil

record.tranche_reason: The study measures benchmark negative log-likelihood across model sizes and fits parameter-scaling curves, but uses downstream benchmark losses rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy, extrapolation to much larger runs, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Table 2 reports downstream benchmark negative log-likelihoods for three sizes and two architectures; Tables 3–4 report fitted coefficients and goodness of fit. The study states that the models use the same fixed token count, but does not state the count.
record.test_reason: The study trains Transformer and 2-simplicial MoE models at 1B, 2B and 3.5B active parameters on a fixed token count. It reports benchmark negative log-likelihood (NLL) at each size and fits log-log parameter exponents per architecture and benchmark. These are its own scaling results in a new setting (MoE, downstream-benchmark NLL), bearing on V6 and V7. They are not pretraining-loss sweeps.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that 2-simplicial attention lowers benchmark NLL at 2B and 3.5B active parameters, with no gain below 2B. They say it raises the parameter exponent α, more so on less saturated benchmarks (MMLU-pro, GSM8k). They argue this suggests tokens could scale slower than parameters, unlike Chinchilla, and favours token-constrained regimes.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares downstream benchmark negative log-likelihood for two attention architectures at fixed token count, rather than fitting held-out pretraining loss across parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported exponent varies with attention architecture and benchmark; the study also states that gains are not seen below 2.0B active parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: The study claims that changing the attention mechanism raises the parameter-scaling exponent, not just the offset. Prior work had held that most architecture changes only shift the offset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture changes (attention type) can alter scaling exponents, not only offsets.

record.problems: Only three active-parameter sizes are tested. The fits use downstream benchmark negative log-likelihood rather than held-out pretraining loss, and the token count is not given. The authors approximate the fixed-token loss relation by ignoring the data term and use active parameters for N.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is reported.
No extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
No compute sweep or optimal N/D allocation. The claim that tokens can grow slower than parameters is speculative and not measured.
No depth, width or shape variation at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime.
Predictability from pretraining loss; accuracy metrics; more than three sizes; any prediction of held-out sizes.
Parameter counting (active vs total), schedule, data, fitting method, and bending away from a single power law.

record.verdict_notes: Only three sizes, and the token count is unstated. The fit drops the irreducible-loss term, approximating log L as linear in log N, and uses active parameters of MoE models. Exponent differences rest on NLL gaps of about 0.2–2% with no error bars. The T2 rows' cross-architecture baselines are method comparisons; for scaling versions the relevant baseline is the smaller same-architecture model. V4 is not tested: attention type is not a shape change at fixed parameter count.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is reported.
The study does not test whether fits on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
No compute-budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is evaluated.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is tested.
Tests benchmark negative log-likelihood across parameter sizes, but not predictability from pretraining loss or other downstream metrics.

Tests whether fitted parameter exponents differ between two attention architectures under this setup. It does not vary parameter counting, training schedule, data, or fitting method, and does not test curves bending away from a power law.

relationships.condition: Transformer and 2-simplicial MoE, 1B→2B→3.5B active params, fixed tokens, NLL on GSM8k/MMLU/MMLU-pro/MBPP
relationships.reason: Benchmark NLL falls monotonically with size in every series (T2-2B-*, T2-3.5B-*), and log-log fits give R2≥0.996 (T4-*). Weak evidence: only three points.
relationships.display_finding: Negative log-likelihood decreased at each of three tested sizes in every series, with log-log fits achieving R²≥0.996.

relationships.condition: Two attention architectures, four benchmarks, 3-point fits on active params at fixed tokens
relationships.reason: Fitted α differs by architecture (6.8–20.2% higher for 2-simplicial) and by benchmark (0.09–0.17) (T3-*). No uncertainty is given on α.
relationships.display_finding: Fitted α is 6.8–20.2% higher for 2-simplicial attention and ranges from 0.09 to 0.17 across benchmarks, without reported exponent uncertainty.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
